summary: Junior Astronaut Lunar Base Mission Trainer is an interactive, web-based simulation game designed for students aged 10–13. As commander of a lunar base at Shackleton Crater near the Moon’s South Pole, players manage a daily solar power budget across three interconnected systems—Life Support, Hydroponic Food Production, and Lunar Science Experiments—across a 7-day mission cycle featuring unexpected challenges like food germination issues and equipment malfunctions.     The project addresses the NASA Space Apps Challenge by translating complex lunar science into accessible, gamified STEM learning. Our simulation models real lunar environmental telemetry derived from NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter and the LADEE mission. Players directly encounter authentic lunar phenomena such as temperatures dipping to -160°C due to shadows in the crater, and electrostatic dust levitation coating solar arrays.    This project is important because future scientists and engineers learn best through hands-on exploration. Instead of ending the game, system failures pause the mission to explain what went wrong and why. This encourages players to test new ideas and adapt. By combining real space data with interactive problem-solving, the trainer shows young learners how space exploration works and inspires them to become the next pioneers of the Moon and beyond
details:
Junior Astronaut Lunar Base Mission Trainer is an interactive web simulation where students aged 10–13 take command of an outpost at Shackleton Crater near the Moon’s South Pole. Across a 7-day lunar cycle, players allocate a constrained daily solar power budget (PU) across three core systems using sliders:

- Life Support (ECLSS): Heats and pressurizes the habitat while recycling cabin air and water.

- Food Production (Hydroponic Bio-Dome): Powers LED grow lights and nutrient pumps to feed the crew and generate oxygen.

- Lunar Science Experiments: Powers ice-core drilling and surface research.

Key mechanics include:

- Biological Symbiosis: Keeping hydroponics above 70% yields a +4% daily life support bonus via photosynthesis; falling below 30% cuts science output in half.

- Thermal & Environmental Drain: Plunging shadow temperatures (down to −160°C) accelerate loss of heat.

- Dynamic Mission Events: Unpredictable challenges—dust levitation, micrometeoroid solar damage, scrubber faults, and surprise crew arrivals—require mid-mission adaptation.

- Fail-Forward Learning: System failures trigger an "Engineering Debrief" explaining the root science and offering an immediate retry.

Key benefits:

- Experiential STEM Learning: Students discover the delicate trade-offs of space systems engineering through hands-on decision-making rather than passive reading.

- NASA Data-Grounded: Briefings, temperatures, and dust conditions reflect authentic lunar mission telemetry.

- Low Barriers: Runs directly in any web browser on classroom Chromebooks, tablets, or desktops without installs or accounts.

Intended impact of the project: To inspire middle-school students during the crucial 10–13 age window when interest in STEM takes root. By demystifying life support (ECLSS), extreme thermal environments, and science experiments, the mission trainer connects real headline space exploration with age appropriate physics and biology.

We believe that our project is creative by merging a realistic NASA flight director dashboard with kid-friendly explanations, such as the Engineer’s Notebook: End-of-day scientific debriefs explaining how real NASA engineers solve each day's exact challenge.

Factors that we considered:

- Intuitive Design: Whole-number power units and color-coded meters (green, amber, pulsing red) keeps the information intuitive for 10–13 year-olds.

- Authentic Physics: modeling the Moon’s sharp divide between illuminated crater rims and very cold shadows.

- Classroom Fit: A brisk 10–15 minute play loop that could fit naturally inside a single class period.

- Universal Design: High-contrast typography and responsive layouts optimized for both small phone viewports and classroom displays.

The Loveable app/website was used to code the application. It was the easiest and simplest way to achieve our goals, especially with no one on the team having any coding experience.
